stops.name: Riverside Drive: the house of paintings
stops.campa: Into a high apartment above the Hudson, Julius Oppenheimer the textile importer and his wife Ella, a painter with a gloved and hidden hand, receive a son. He is Julius Robert, born to money and to pictures: Van Gogh and Cézanne and a Rembrandt hang on the walls, servants move in the rooms, and the great river runs below. The child is delicate, precocious, and lonely, a boy who will collect the mineral kingdom before he learns to fight. The house holds him like a cabinet of wonders. From these rooms the whole arc begins.

stops.name: The Ethical Culture School: Deed before Creed
stops.campa: At seven he enters Felix Adler's school on Central Park West, where God is not spoken but conduct is everything and the motto reads Deed before Creed. Here the non-observant Jewish boy is given a moral universe without a heaven: reason, service, the ethical act as its own altar. He devours English and French, physics, mineralogy. Teachers mark him strange and brilliant. The creed of the deed sinks into him and will never leave; it is the same conscience that later stands, torn, before the bomb. The school forges the moral instrument.
stops.quote_source: Motto of the New York Society for Ethical Culture (Felix Adler)

stops.name: The New York Mineralogical Club: the boy who read a paper
stops.campa: The child rockhound writes letters to the great mineralogists of the city in a hand so learned that the New York Mineralogical Club invites him to speak, not knowing he is twelve. He stands on a stack of crates to reach the lectern and delivers his paper on the crystalline forms, and the grey-bearded members applaud a schoolboy. Kunz himself presides. The collecting fever, labels, cleavage planes, the geometry hidden in stone, is the first sign of the ordering mind that will later array the elements of the earth toward fission.

stops.name: Joachimsthal: the mines, the dysentery, the delayed start
stops.campa: Graduated from Ethical Culture at seventeen and prizewinning, he is sent by a beloved teacher into the mountains of Bohemia to prospect for minerals: to Joachimsthal, the old silver and pitchblende valley whose ore has just given the Curies their radium and lent its name, thaler, to the dollar. There in the mines he falls gravely ill with dysentery; he comes home wasted, too sick to enter Harvard, and the year is lost to convalescence. The boy who will split the atom sickens, by chance, in the very valley from which the uranium first came. The threads begin to knot.

stops.name: Harvard College: chemistry, and the turn to physics
stops.campa: He arrives in Cambridge, Massachusetts a year late, recovered from the dysentery that felled him in Germany, and falls upon Harvard like a starving man. He majors in chemistry but is seized by Percy Bridgman's thermodynamics; he reads insatiably in six subjects at once, poetry and Sanskrit-adjacent philosophy alongside the sciences, calling himself a 'hot house' of ambition. He is friendless and intense, given to what he names his 'beastly' moods. In three years he takes the degree summa cum laude: the flame burning far ahead of the flesh.
stops.quote: My feeling about myself was always one of extreme discontent.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer, recalling his youth (Bird & Sherwin, American Prometheus)

stops.name: Perro Caliente: the ranch in the Sangre de Cristo
stops.campa: Summers he rides the high country of northern New Mexico, and on a rented cabin in the Pecos wilderness of the Sangre de Cristo he shouts 'Hot dog!' And the place is named Perro Caliente. On horseback through the aspen and the thin blue air he finds the two loves that will fuse in his fate: physics and the desert of New Mexico. 'My two great loves are physics and desert country,' he writes; 'it's a pity they can't be combined.' Two decades later he will combine them, on a mesa he can nearly see from here.
stops.quote: My two great loves are physics and desert country. It's a pity they can't be combined.

stops.name: The Cavendish Laboratory: the failure of the hands
stops.campa: At the Cavendish under J. J. Thomson and Rutherford, Oppenheimer discovers a cruel truth: he cannot do experiment. His hands are clumsy at the bench, his soul aches for theory, and the laboratory that is the temple of the atom becomes his torment. He is homesick, jealous, near unravelling; he confesses to friends that he is 'on the point of bumping myself off.' The finest theoretical mind of his generation sits blocking glassware and hating it, and the misery gathers toward a single, poisoned act.
stops.quote: I am having a pretty bad time. The lab work is a terrible bore, and I am so bad at it that it is impossible to feel that I am learning anything.

stops.name: The poisoned apple: left for Patrick Blackett
stops.campa: His tutor is Patrick Blackett, handsome, athletic, everything Oppenheimer is not, who drives him toward the bench he loathes. In a fit of envy and breakdown he laces an apple with chemicals and lays it on Blackett's desk. Blackett never eats it. The deed is discovered; the University moves toward a charge of attempted murder, and only his father's frantic intervention saves him: probation, and a psychiatrist. The genius has tried to kill his teacher with a poisoned fruit. It is the first of his doublings: the maker of death, refusing his own dark hand.

stops.name: Corsica: the island that lifted the darkness
stops.campa: Three analysts fail him; one names dementia praecox and gives him up. Then, on a bicycle tour of Corsica reading Proust by flashlight in a mountain inn, the cloud breaks. Later he calls it not a love affair but love itself: 'a great thing in my life, a great and lasting part of it.' On the maquis-scented island the self-hatred loosens; he chooses to live. The introspective literature does what the doctors could not. He rides down to the boats a man reassembled, and turns toward Germany and the new physics.
stops.quote: Not a mere love affair, not a love affair at all, but love… a great thing in my life, a great and lasting part of it.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer, on Corsica (Bird & Sherwin, American Prometheus)

stops.name: Göttingen: Max Born and the ferment
stops.campa: He comes to the little Saxon town that is, in this hour, the throbbing centre of the quantum revolution. Born teaches, Heisenberg passes through, Dirac and Pauli and Fermi and the young Teller argue in the seminars. Oppenheimer talks too much, seizes the blackboard, dominates until Maria Goeppert circulates a petition to make the American be quiet. But the mind is dazzling now, released from the bench, at home at last in pure theory. In this ferment the shy failed experimentalist becomes a physicist of the first rank.

stops.name: The doctorate: the Born–Oppenheimer approximation
stops.campa: At twenty-three he takes his Ph.D. under Born, and with him publishes the paper that separates the slow heavy nuclei from the fast electrons in a molecule: the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, still taught a century on. His examiner James Franck emerges saying he was glad it was over, for Oppenheimer had begun to ask the questions. The name is now welded into the language of physics. The instrument is finished, tempered, and sharp; it wants only a country and a war to be turned to its terrible use.

stops.name: Leiden: where he becomes 'Opje'
stops.campa: On a fellowship he comes to Leiden, to Paul Ehrenfest, the Socratic gadfly of physics, and astonishes the Dutch by lecturing in a Dutch he has learned in weeks. The students, charmed, give him the affectionate name Opje, which his Berkeley disciples will later anglicize to Oppie, and it clings to him for life. Ehrenfest, wary of his showy brilliance, sends him not to the gentle Bohr but to the fierce Pauli in Zurich, to have the flashiness ground away. The wandering scholar collects tongues and masters as easily as once he collected stones.
